papers.title: What does quantum parameter estimation estimate? A no-go result for true quantity values
papers.abstract: We examine the conditions under which quantum parameter estimation is compatible with the concept of a ``true'' quantity value: a unique value of the estimated quantity that exists prior to and independently of measurement. While quantum parameter estimation typically assumes that the quantity to be estimated is a parameter, we argue that this assumption can be lifted, opening the way to a more general formulation of estimation that may apply even in situations where the quantity to be estimated is no longer a parameter, but instead a quantum variable susceptible to quantum fluctuations. We identify three assumptions that characterize the way estimation is often presented in the quantum metrology literature, namely, as a procedure for inferring an unknown ``true value", which is assumed to be unique and to exist prior to and independently of measurement. Using our more general framework, we prove a no-go theorem showing that the preceding assumptions are jointly incompatible with two further assumptions: the completeness of the quantum state (no `hidden variables'), and the presence of entanglement between the probe systems and the system under measurement. We note that the presence of such entanglement is a generic prediction of standard quantum theory. Consequently, if one is not willing to accept hidden variables, nor willing to modify standard quantum theory by introducing a new physical mechanism that destroys entanglement at some scale or regime, then a realist account of estimation is ultimately impossible.

papers.title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
papers.abstract: We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.

papers.title: Mixed State Deep Thermalization under Generic Quantum Errors
papers.abstract: Pure-state deep thermalization predicts that, after sufficient scrambling, projected ensembles approach universal distributions that contain information beyond the reduced density matrix. In realistic quantum systems, however, noise is unavoidable and the projected states are generally mixed. Whether mixed-state deep thermalization admits an analogous universal limiting distribution has remained unclear. Here we answer this question for quantum dynamics containing local quantum channels, i.e., errors. We show that the late-time mixed-state projected ensemble is completely determined by the normalized Choi state of the error channel and is universal, independent of the microscopic details of the underlying unitary dynamics. We establish this result analytically for dual-unitary circuits, global Haar-random dynamics, and local Haar-random circuits at large local dimension, and verify it numerically in qubit circuits and kicked Ising dynamics. In a solvable setting, we further find exponentially fast convergence to the limiting ensemble. Our results extend deep thermalization to noisy quantum dynamics and establish a direct correspondence between quantum errors and universal random mixed-state ensembles.

papers.title: Size-independent Logarithmic Sobolev Inequalities for Quantum Gibbs Samplers
papers.abstract: We propose a new method for proving $L^2$ and modified logarithmic Sobolev inequalities with constants independent of system size for quantum Gibbs samplers whose Lindblad generators satisfy Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) detailed balance. We first establish the $L^2$ logarithmic Sobolev inequality by transporting it along a temperature-dependent path from the infinite-temperature product state to the target Gibbs state while maintaining a size-independent decay rate for the sandwiched Rényi-2 divergence. A tensor-power argument, combined with the quantum asymptotic equipartition property, then transfers this decay bound to relative entropy, yielding the modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality. This approach provides a general framework for proving size-independent logarithmic Sobolev inequalities for quantum Gibbs samplers. We apply it to two regimes: one-dimensional quantum spin chains at every finite temperature, and finite-range quantum spin systems at sufficiently high temperature in any fixed dimension.

papers.title: ArcTN: Efficient Tensor-Network Contraction Planning for Quantum Circuit Simulation
papers.abstract: Tensor-network simulation of quantum circuits depends on contraction orders with low computational cost and small intermediate tensors, found without excessive planning time. We present ArcTN, a contraction-order optimization framework with two search presets. Light keeps planning overhead low, and Heavy spends more effort on refinement. Both combine randomized-greedy construction, subtree reconfiguration, and parallel tempering with stage-specific stopping rules. ArcTN also provides Fixed and Dynamic slicing to meet tensor-size limits and executes the returned orders. On the 30 QC32 quantum-circuit networks completed by all eight compared configurations, Light reduces FLOPs by 61.32% and plans 1.62$\times$ faster than Cotengra Auto/CMA-ES, and Heavy reduces FLOPs by 43.83% and plans 7.21$\times$ faster than Cotengra AutoHQ/Optuna. Heavy also needs 11.85% fewer FLOPs than OMECO TreeSA-8 and plans 1.33$\times$ faster. Dynamic slicing meets the size limits in all 90 runs on 18 scalar-output networks and reduces total sliced FLOPs by 31.99% relative to Fixed slicing, at the cost of longer planning. With a common NumPy executor, Heavy has the lowest combined planning and execution time among five configurations on the runs that all of them completed. On 672 networks built from 320 MQT Bench circuits, Heavy obtains the lowest geometric-mean FLOPs on the 142 large networks while planning 3.1$\times$ and 31$\times$ faster than Cotengra AutoHQ and Hyper128.

papers.title: Problem-aware sampling for bias and variance reduction in randomised Hamiltonian simulation
papers.abstract: Randomised quantum simulation algorithms such as qDRIFT reduce circuit depth by replacing deterministic product formulas with stochastic compilations, but achieving high accuracy can require many steps. In vanilla qDRIFT, Hamiltonian terms are sampled with probabilities proportional to their coefficient magnitudes. We propose StateDRIFT, a variant of qDRIFT which optimises its sampling distribution to estimate time-evolved quantities using knowledge of the initial state and target observable, with a provable truncation bound that keeps qDRIFT's guarantees. The distribution at each depth is chosen by solving an optimisation problem targeting bias and/or variance. StateDRIFT can significantly reduce the bias and variance of estimators, and hence circuit depth, which we test on short-time dynamics of lattice models and molecules under Jordan-Wigner up to 18 qubits. For example, with BeH2 StateDRIFT can reduce the number of two-qubit gates required to achieve a given accuracy from 11,201 to 983. StateDRIFT involves measuring observables and commutators on the initial state, so we propose two practical ways to estimate these: classical surrogates such as tensor networks, and classical shadows, which recover most or all of the saving from exact oracles in the systems tested.

papers.title: One-shot entanglement generation and distillation via Petz recovery and binary hypothesis testing
papers.abstract: How much entanglement can two distant laboratories share when their connection is noisy? We relate this question to deciding which of two quantum hypotheses is present. Our one-shot bounds apply to entanglement generation over a quantum channel and to one-way entanglement distillation from a shared state. We use Cheng's trace inequality to bound the infidelity of a Petz decoder in terms of a binary hypothesis testing cost. Applying the inequality before averaging over codes reduces the error analysis to computing a second moment of random subspaces. The proof covers every integer target dimension and treats rank-deficient states explicitly. A corollary expresses the achievable entanglement through hypothesis-testing coherent information, with a single logarithmic error slack and exact integer rounding. We also prove an error-preserving conversion from entanglement generation codes to entanglement transmission codes: the target dimension decreases by only a constant factor at fixed error, and the decoder is the original decoder followed by local processing. Consequently, for both entanglement generation and entanglement transmission, arbitrary pure reference-input states yield the same coherent-information rate, second-order Gaussian correction at the original error tolerance, and explicit achievable logarithmic remainder. For commuting testing hypotheses, the logarithmic remainder improves to a constant. These results give a direct route from binary distinguishability to explicit recovery guarantees and finite-resource quantum communication rates.

papers.title: The Impact of Markovian Errors on Random Circuits
papers.abstract: Randomized benchmarking (RB) returns a single decay parameter or gate error rate, but when the noise is gate-dependent that parameter is notoriously difficult to interpret. We study RB and related random-circuit benchmarks under small gate-local Markovian noise by factorizing each noisy gate into its ideal action followed by the exponential of a small error generator and then perturbing the RB $\mathscr{L}$ matrix, which models the RB decay. For any low-error gate set that satisfies the requirements of RB (it is a sequence-asymptotic unitary 2-design), we show that Pauli-stochastic error rates contribute linearly to the RB decay parameter, while Hamiltonian error rates contribute through a gauge-invariant quadratic form. Pauli-correlation and active generators are absent from the linear term and enter only at higher order. For the single-qubit native gate set $\{X_{π/2},Y_{π/2}\}$ we derive this quadratic form explicitly in terms of three first-order gauge-invariant (FOGI) coordinates: the two intrinsic over-rotations and one relational axis-tilt error. The resulting formula explains the dependence of DRB on the sampling distribution and the compilation dependence of CRB. These results turn RB decay rates into interpretable functions of experimentally meaningful elementary error rates.

papers.title: Nanopillar metasurfaces uniting high optical reflectivity with ultracoherent nanomechanics
papers.abstract: Mechanically compliant mirrors are key components in cavity optomechanics. However, the requirements to achieve the best optical and mechanical performance are usually in direct competition. A high reflectivity for tightly focused beams entails thick reflectors, whereas ultracoherent flexural nanomechanics necessitates thin membranes. We eliminate this trade-off by introducing high-refractive-index nanopillar metasurfaces on top of a thin membrane. We pattern a 50 micrometer-diameter array of nanopillars to form a photonic crystal. The flat band behavior of guided resonances in the photonic crystal enables a reflectivity of 99.82(1)% for a tightly focused beam of 7 micrometer waist. The combination of two guided resonances creates a 100 nanometer-wide high-reflectivity band around 1550 nanometer. Simultaneously, the nanopillar patterning realizes a density-modulated phononic crystal that isolates an ultracoherent localized mechanical mode with a $Q\cdot f$-product of $2\cdot 10^{14}$Hz. The demonstrated nanopillar metasurfaces enable lightweight mirrors for room-temperature quantum optomechanics and for use as levitated mirrors or lightsails.

papers.title: ConQEC: Concolic Testing for Quantum Error-Correcting Code Implementations
papers.abstract: Quantum error-correcting code (QECC) implementations are hybrid software-control systems: measured syndromes drive decoder dispatch, recovery actions, and logical checks. Existing QECC verification techniques can prove formal obligations, and general quantum testing can expose final failures, but developers still lack a scalable testing workflow that generates concrete faults and explains where a QECC repair path first diverges. This paper presents ConQEC, to our knowledge the first concolic testing framework for QECC implementations. By combining concrete (Pauli) fault replay with symbolic repair-path constraints, ConQEC generates tests that expose not only final logical failures but also fault--syndrome--decoder--recovery (FSDR) diagnostics: the injected fault, observed syndrome, decoder decision, recovery action, oracle result, and earliest divergent stage. Its symbolic encoding of Pauli faults, syndrome predicates, decoder and recovery relations, and oracle checks enables this diagnostic workflow to scale beyond exponentially increasing amplitude-level quantum-state reasoning. We implemented ConQEC and evaluated it on generated source-level QECC families and public QECC artifacts with up to thousands of qubits. ConQEC detects the seeded bug in every experimental case and reports a replay-valid, fault-localizing FSDR witness for each.

papers.title: Nonlinear quantum noise polarization in macroscopic nonlinear QED
papers.abstract: We construct a quantum theory of light in nonlinearly responding materials with dispersion and absorption and, in particular, show the emergence of non-Gaussian noise associated with nonlinear absorption processes. Our theory is based on a path-integral formulation of the microscopic Huttner-Barnett model including cubic matter self-interaction required for $χ^{(2)}$ nonlinear processes. We show that the noise polarization emerges naturally from a decoupling of the stochastic weights of the bath response which, in case of cubic self-interactions, leads to a decoupling via Airy functions. As the theory is, by construction, consistent with the nonlinear fluctuation-dissipation theorem, it constitutes a viable quantum theory of light in nonlinear media.

papers.title: Predictive electronic feedback control for narrow-linewidth lasers
papers.abstract: Narrow-linewidth lasers are essential for various key atom-laser interaction processes and optical setups in quantum coherent control, quantum precision measurement, and quantum information science. The Pound-Drever-Hall (PDH) technique is the standard method for the frequency-stabilization of narrow-linewidth lasers, but the inherent time delay in its feedback loop inevitably induces excessive phase noise, commonly known as servo bumps. Previous solutions primarily rely on additional optical components outside the electronic feedback control loop. Here, we propose and implement a generic method based on the Smith predictor to address the time-delay issue entirely within the electronic part of the PDH feedback control loop. We systematically demonstrate its capability to suppress phase noise and reduce servo bumps by adding only a single Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) controller to the loop. This class of methods is demonstrated to be conceptually concise with minimal hardware overhead, effective in practice, and holds potential for a wide variety of future applications.

papers.title: Krylov Complexity and Entropy of Composite Quantum Systems
papers.abstract: We investigate the behaviour of Krylov complexity as the number of degrees of freedom of a quantum system increases. Specifically, we show that for tensor products of commuting subsystems, the leading excess complexity is controlled by a weighted variance of the subsystem Lanczos coefficients. This provides a quantitative measure of dynamical heterogeneity and a precise characterization of synchronous evolution. We also show that Krylov entropy is able to disambiguate the information associated with subsystems composition from that generated by dynamical mismatch, and that the same Lanczos variance controls the leading mismatch contribution to both complexity and the entropy. Our results establish excess complexity and Krylov entropy as complementary probes of the emergence of collective dynamics in large quantum systems.

papers.title: Qubits Are Not Enough: Deflation and Measurement Limits in Variational Quantum Modal Analysis
papers.abstract: Amplitude encoding stores an N-degree-of-freedom structural mode using ceiling(log2 N) qubits. This article develops an evaluation framework for variational quantum eigensolvers in finite-element structural dynamics. A Cholesky transformation maps the generalized eigenproblem to a symmetric mass-orthonormal Hamiltonian, ensuring Euclidean quantum-state orthogonality equals structural mass orthogonality. For higher modes, the deflation penalty condition is sharpened to a necessary-and-sufficient threshold, with a Davis-Kahan bound quantifying effects of approximate projectors. Numerical studies separate mapping correctness, ansatz expressibility, preprocessing, Pauli growth, finite-shot uncertainty, and damage localization. For 128-DOF chains, consistent-mass whitening increases transformed-operator density from 0.023 to 0.308 and Pauli terms from 576 to 2950. Exact state-vector experiments show qubit count and circuit expressibility are distinct. At 10^5 shots per Pauli term, first-mode frequency RMS error is 2.45%. In an oracle-state study, 10% stiffness loss is localized in 84.5% of trials. Results sharpen the deflation condition, quantify resource bottlenecks, and claim no speedup.

papers.title: Orbital-coherence memory in electrical transport and its self-consistent Maxwell response
papers.abstract: An internal electronic coherence changes electrical transport only when it feeds back on the physical current. We develop a reduced description of this feedback and distinguish its exact consequences from the assumptions required for a microscopic realization. An opposite-parity two-orbital Hamiltonian identifies a current-coupled orbital force. Under an explicitly stated moment closure and collision ansatz, it yields a passive three-state response with an exponentially damped oscillatory memory. The resulting conductivity redistributes a fixed optical weight and predicts a nonmonotonic dependence of dc conduction on coherence damping at fixed remaining parameters. The orbital reduction constrains the coupling and internal frequency through a shared bare splitting, providing a test beyond unconstrained spectral fitting. A charge-conserving spatial extension couples to Maxwell equations through a positive energy balance and separates the constitutive response from longitudinal collective and transverse electromagnetic modes. We formulate complex-conductivity and transmission tests, including the limits of parameter identification over a finite bandwidth. The model supplies a conditional connection between orbital dynamics, transport memory, and electromagnetic observables; conductivity alone does not establish a uniquely quantum mechanism, and a material-specific collision calculation and closure-error assessment remain necessary.

papers.title: Finite Systems in the Space of Projective Measurements
papers.abstract: We investigate the dynamics of two-level systems using the quasidistribution $Q$ function projected onto the space of collective measurements. Particular attention is given to evolution under Hamiltonians that are invariant under particle permutations, for pure states that are either invariant or noninvariant under such permutations. This requires constructing an approximate analog of the star product between quasidistribution functions: the projected $Q$ function of a product of two operators is expressed approximately in terms of the individual operators' $Q$ and $P$ functions. We rewrite the Liouville equation to determine approximate state dynamics and compare the result with exact evolution using the Hellinger distance. Overall, the method performs well for permutation-invariant pure states and Hamiltonians, whereas deviations arise for arbitrary pure states and noninvariant Hamiltonians.

papers.title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents
papers.abstract: Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.

papers.title: Quantum Fokker-Planck solvers as trainable generative models
papers.abstract: We develop and analyze generative models based on quantum solvers of stochastic differential equations. Unlike the common approach based on layered variational quantum circuits with parameterized rotations, we parameterize the potential of a Langevin process. The associated Fokker-Planck (FP) equations are Hermitianized and solved using a linear combination of cosine operators implemented through quantum singular value transformation. By encoding the square root of the stationary density, the model enables sampling through computational-basis measurements and is efficiently controlled by coefficients of the block-encoded diagonal potential. We train the proposed model to match empirical distributions within the family described by FP equations, demonstrating parameter recovery for multivariate probability distributions. Crucially, the model remains trainable at scale. Sample-efficient and convex optimization for in-distribution targets arises from a physics-informed inductive bias and holds regardless of the dimensionality of the problem. We provide circuit constructions and efficient block encodings of the main components of the algorithm and analyze resource requirements. Our approach frames quantum generative learning as quantum model discovery and provides a foundation for extending this framework to high-dimensional, strongly correlated scientific data.

papers.title: High-fidelity entanglement of two spectrally-distinct solid state emitters
papers.abstract: Solid state quantum emitters with electronic spin properties can be entangled using optical interferometric which-path erasure techniques that rely on identical frequencies and linewidths of the emitters. This promises a powerful, fast and scalable platform for quantum technologies. Using current protocols, a pair of emitters embedded in a waveguide interferometer can be deterministically prepared in a maximally entangled state. However, the amount of entanglement diminishes rapidly with increasing separation of the emission lines and variations in the linewidths of the emitters. Solid state emitters such as quantum dots are subject to intrinsic variations in the fabrication process. Therefore, manufacturing the required number of identical emitters on a chip is not scalable. In this Letter, we present a method that uses readily available pairs of entangled photons to entangle solid state emitters with large transition frequency separations and linewidth variations, circumventing the need to fabricate optically identical emitters. We demonstrate a concurrence of C = 0.95 for typical quantum dots using narrowband photon inputs.

papers.title: Rank-One Loss Maximizes the Spectral Response Strength of Passive Full-Order Exceptional Points
papers.abstract: We consider finite-dimensional non-Hermitian systems in which all modes coalesce at a single exceptional point. For a rank-one anti-Hermitian contribution, the spectral response strength is computed exactly. For passive systems, we then derive a sharp upper bound at fixed exceptional-point decay rate and show that it is reached only when the decay operator has rank one, corresponding to a single independent dissipative direction. This establishes rank-one loss as the optimal configuration for enhancing the response of a full-order exceptional point. The bound holds for arbitrary order and improves on earlier passive estimates beyond second order. Two third-order trimers illustrate the result: a rank-one-loss system saturates the bound, whereas a passive rank-two-loss realization remains below it. The result turns dissipation into a design resource: concentrating the loss into a single effective dissipative direction maximizes the highest-order spectral response of a passive full-order exceptional-point device.

papers.title: Can Entanglement-Induced Feature-Map Designs Improve Projected Quantum Kernels?
papers.abstract: Projected quantum kernels (PQKs) have emerged as a notable approach to circumvent the hardness of machine learning tasks arising from the exponential dimensionality of the quantum Hilbert space. However, recent PQK studies often rely heavily on extensive classical hyperparameter tuning of the radial basis function (RBF) kernel parameter and the support vector machine regularization parameter. The extensive tuning can mask the true representational power of the underlying PQKs induced by quantum feature maps, which has not been explored in detail. Thus, this work aims to expose the structural capabilities of PQKs by isolating and evaluating their native inductive bias through comparisons between untuned and tuned PQKs against the RBF baseline. Furthermore, we propose novel quantum feature maps that leverage two-qubit entanglement to capture multivariate correlations in IoT data. The results show that extensive tuning can lead to competitive performance architectures, while our proposed entanglement topologies exhibit a significantly stronger native inductive bias. This reveals that superior quantum architectural design can yield structurally better PQKs with improvements arising from quantum-mechanical properties rather than from classical hyperparameter tuning.

papers.title: Reset-Enhanced Dissipative Quantum Metrology
papers.abstract: Quantum metrology is ultimately shaped not only by measurements, but also by the dissipative dynamics that prepare and maintain the probe. Nevertheless, a general mechanism for enhancing both steady-state and transient precision in open quantum systems has been lacking. Here we show that adding a simple reset channel provides such a mechanism: reset acts as a minimal dissipative control that can enhance metrological precision without modifying the intrinsic Hamiltonian or applying continuous coherent driving. We derive a unified quantum-Fisher-information (QFI) reset-rate response identity, showing how reset enhances steady-state and transient estimation while revealing a sharp transient distinction. For static-parameter estimation in diagonal dynamics, reset leaves the leading short-time QFI unchanged; for the separate task of elapsed-time estimation, it generates an immediate drift contribution that can scale quadratically with the reset rate in the short-time limit. For frequency estimation, the enhancement is instead dominated by a genuinely quantum eigenvector contribution. These results establish reset as a simple dissipative resource for open-system quantum metrology.

papers.title: Fluctuation-free Quantum Battery Charging Enabled by Bell-like Entangled and Separable Charger States
papers.abstract: The implication of entanglement in quantum battery charging remains poorly understood. In addition, intrinsic quantum randomness poses a fundamental challenge to charging uniformity across distinct trials. To address these issues, we study a three-qubit system within a cascaded collision frame, with two qubits acting as the charger and the third serving as the battery. After each collision, an adaptive measurement is performed on the charger, yielding four conditional post-measurement battery states with identical expected stored energy. For arbitrary fixed charger states, we derive analytical expressions for the recurrence relation of stored energy. We find that stored-energy fluctuations depend on whether the dynamics relies on the battery phase \(γ_n\). For two Bell-like families of entangled states, together with their computational basis states termed Bell-like separable states, the dynamics is \(γ_n\)-independent and fluctuations vanish, whereas for other entangled and separable states, fluctuations emerge. These insights establish a paradigm for engineering charger states to design uniform-charging quantum-battery architectures despite inherent quantum randomness.

papers.title: Local Dephasing Sustains Continuous Time Crystals in a Spin-1/2 Ensemble
papers.abstract: Local pure dephasing suppresses single-spin coherence, yet we show that it sustains continuous time-crystalline order in a fully connected ferromagnetic spin-$1/2$ ensemble with local decay. An exact operator identity reveals the mechanism: dephasing raises the interaction energy, while energy relaxation on a finite timescale converts this charging into delayed feedback. Within homogeneous mean-field theory, we prove that dephasing is necessary for periodic motion in this model and that feedback exactly balances transverse damping over each cycle. Beyond mean field, the identity fixes the relative amplitude and phase of energy and longitudinal magnetization in oscillatory Liouvillian modes. Liouvillian spectra and stationary two-time correlations characterize temporal order through decay rates that decrease algebraically with system size, frequencies approaching nonzero mean-field values, and comparable per-spin oscillatory weights. Semiclassical trajectories further reveal recurrent switching between a limit-cycle region and two symmetry-related stationary regions: fluctuations interrupt and reactivate collective oscillations, and oscillatory episodes provide an intermediate channel between stationary regions. These results establish local dephasing as a resource for autonomous collective motion and show how the resulting temporal order can participate in metastable dynamics.

papers.title: Entanglement certification of attosecond light fields with photoelectron interferometry
papers.abstract: The emergence of entangled quantum optical states in high-harmonic generation raises a fundamental problem about its characterization, namely, \textit{how can entanglement of extreme-ultraviolet radiation be certified for attosecond light fields?} Here, we provide experimentally accessible separability tests, particularly showing that attosecond photoelectron interferometry provides a direct solution to this problem. This is achieved by a quantum optical treatment of mapping photoelectron interferometry to the measurement of optical correlation functions. This yields a negative-partial-transpose witness for infrared-XUV entanglement and a sufficient witness of genuine multipartite entanglement without auxiliary optical measurements. We evaluate both witnesses on explicit optical states and identify how the protocol can be extended to XUV-XUV entanglement certification. Hence, we establish attosecond photoelectron interferometry as a general framework for entanglement certification across a wide range of optical frequencies.

papers.title: Realization of a Superleak in a Quantum Gas
papers.abstract: Ultracold quantum gases offer a controllable and microscopically accessible platform for understanding and engineering superfluidity. Yet, realizing a superleak that selectively transports the superfluid while suppressing normal flow has remained elusive. Here, we harness an optical superlattice to realize such a superleak through dynamical selectivity. The superfluid undergoes coherent Josephson transport, whereas the normal component exhibits slow, thermodynamically limited response, resulting in a flow-rate contrast of 500(49). Exploiting this contrast, we demonstrate repeated filtering of the normal component and dynamical purification of the superfluid, while sustaining coherent driven oscillations for up to 100 cycles. Our results establish a controllable atomic superleak and open possibilities for manipulating transport and thermodynamics in quantum fluids.

papers.title: Quantum Constrained Hamiltonian Descent
papers.abstract: We propose Quantum Constrained Hamiltonian Descent (QCHD), a continuous-time quantum framework for optimization under smooth equality constraints. The unconstrained counterpart, Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD), minimizes a cost function by simulating the Schrödinger dynamics of a particle in the potential given by the cost function. Applying Dirac's formalism to the classical dynamics with constraints, we construct an intrinsic quantum Hamiltonian with a Laplace--Beltrami operator on the constraint manifold in a kinetic term. Its evolution preserves the constraints exactly without penalty terms and is expected to solve quantum-dynamically the constrained optimization problem. We analyze its relation to Quantum Hamiltonian Descent supplemented by a strong penalty term. For a squared-distance penalty, the effective tangential dynamics acquires an extrinsic-curvature potential and, in nontrivial normal-rotation sectors, a coupling to the normal-bundle connection. These embedding-dependent terms remain in the strong-penalty limit, generally yielding quantum dynamics different from QCHD. Numerical comparisons for circular, elliptical, and two simultaneous constraints show faster optimization and improved concentration near global minima for the initial states and finite penalty strengths considered.

papers.title: The often overlooked role of sound in liquid thermal transport
papers.abstract: Formulated a hundred years ago, the Bridgman formula for thermal conductivity of liquids postulates a proportionality between sound velocity and thermal conductivity. This designates phonons as heat carriers in a liquid. Its empirical success has been under-appreciated and its conceptual implications overlooked. It is not mentioned in well-known condensed-matter textbook. Here, we review its origin, its links to hydrodynamic Euler equations and to the fundamental paradox surrounding the parabolic heat equation and its fate across the quantum-classical crossover.

papers.title: The limits of magic-state distillation
papers.abstract: Magic-state factories are a major cost of fault-tolerant quantum computing, yet how few noisy inputs they need is known only for restricted protocols. We show that, for tolerating input faults, any stabilizer protocol, however adaptive, postselected or multistage, is no better than a projection onto one stabilizer code, and that for rational targets a fault pattern is harmful exactly when its complement is. Searches over all codes show that quadratic distillation of one T state needs exactly nine inputs and that the eight-input CCZ factory is optimal. At order $d$, one T state needs $n\geq2d$.

papers.title: Norm-Aware Product Formulas for Hamiltonian Simulations
papers.abstract: With the target of efficiently solving the quantum-mechanical Schrödinger equation on future quantum computers, first- and second-order product formulas for the time-evolution operator are proposed, designed to exploit hierarchies in the operator norms of the individual Hamiltonian components. Inspired by the THRIFT product formula, these decomposition schemes achieve a suppression of the leading error term by a factor of alpha<1 with respect to the standard Lie--Trotter--Suzuki splitting of the same order, where alpha quantifies the norm ratio between the dominant and subdominant parts of the Hamiltonian. Unlike THRIFT, the proposed formulas retain the general product-formula structure, making them applicable to Hamiltonians whose terms act on an arbitrary number of qubits. The advantages of this approach are demonstrated through numerical experiments on engineered two-dimensional spin-1/2 XY model systems and isolated molecules within the double-factorization framework.

papers.title: Entanglement transitions and multifractality in monitored free-fermions with random long-range hopping
papers.abstract: We study the entanglement dynamics of a one-dimensional chain of monitored non-interacting complex fermions with random power-law hopping characterized by a decay exponent $α$. For $α\lesssim 1$, in stark contrast with the case of hopping to nearest neighbors, the scaling of the entanglement entropy (EE) of the steady state with system size $L$ is faster than logarithmic for any monitoring or disorder strength and it tends towards a linear (volume-law) scaling for sufficiently small $α\lesssim 1/2$. For $α> 3/2$, the EE is in the area-law phase, namely, no scaling with $L$, for any monitoring strength. For $1 < α\lesssim 3/2$, we identify an $α$-dependent measurement-induced phase transition (MIPT) at a critical value of the monitoring strength separating the mentioned area-law and sub-volume-law phases. At this critical point, the EE scales logarithmically with system size, and the density-density correlation function, closely related to the EE, exhibits multifractal features. These results highlight the importance of superdiffusive classical hopping in the entanglement dynamic of quantum many-body systems and also help differentiate its role with respect to conventional sources of entanglement such as genuine quantum non-locality.

papers.title: A Slice-Rank Drift Bound for Random Quantum \(k\)-SAT
papers.abstract: Random quantum satisfiability is a natural quantum analogue of random constraint satisfaction and a basic model for frustration-free local Hamiltonians. Despite extensive work on its satisfiable and unsatisfiable regimes, the quantitative location of the random quantum \(k\)-SAT threshold has remained poorly understood, with the best general upper bounds leaving a large gap to the known lower bounds. In this paper we prove a new upper bound on the satisfiability threshold of random quantum \(k\)-SAT. Our result improves the previously known asymptotic upper bound by a factor of order \(k\), giving a bound of order \(2^k/k\). The improvement is also significant at small values of \(k\); in particular, for random quantum \(3\)-SAT we obtain a substantially smaller explicit upper bound than the one previously available. The proof combines the geometric formulation of generic quantum satisfiability with a dimension-decay analysis of the full satisfying subspace. The key input is a multiplicative Shearer-type inequality for tensor-product subspaces, which quantifies how global dimension forces nontrivial local dimension on typical sets of qubits.

papers.title: Position measurement of a levitated particle with vectorial light
papers.abstract: We develop a fully vectorial, semiclassical scattering formalism for optically levitated dipolar scatterers, expressed within the angular spectrum representation and applicable to arbitrary trapping-field configurations as well as to high--numerical-aperture focusing. Within this framework, we introduce the information radiation pattern to characterize the angular distribution of position-dependent information and use a Richards--Wolf projection of the scattered field onto the local-oscillator mode to quantify the resulting mode-matching efficiency, yielding experimentally realistic forward- and backward-detection efficiencies. As a worked example, we apply the formalism to a radially polarized trapping beam and confirm that the axial recoil heating rate is reduced relative to a conventional linearly polarized Gaussian tweezer. The theoretical framework is implemented in LevitationToolbox, an open-source Python package intended to support the design and optimization of near-Heisenberg-limited levitated optomechanical experiments.

papers.title: Unified Framework for Bidirectional and Cyclic Teleportation under Noise
papers.abstract: Quantum teleportation has evolved from single-qubit, unidirectional communication to multi-qubit and multidirectional protocols. However, most existing schemes rely on protocol-specific entangled resources, motivating the development of universal quantum channels capable of supporting multiple communication tasks simultaneously. In this work, we demonstrate that a single twelve-qubit entangled channel exhibits such versatility by enabling the bidirectional teleportation of arbitrary three-qubit states and the cyclic teleportation of arbitrary two-qubit states through local Bell-state measurements and single-qubit operations. Both protocols are further generalized to multi-qubit and multi-party configurations, establishing the scalability of the proposed framework. To assess its practical applicability, the protocols are analyzed under amplitude-damping, phase-damping, bit-flip, phase-flip, and depolarizing noise channels by plotting the teleportation fidelity as a function of both the input-state parameters and noise strength. The analysis reveals distinct noise sensitivities, with the bidirectional protocol remaining perfectly faithful under bit-flip noise for all input states and noise strengths, while the cyclic protocol is consistently more vulnerable to environmental disturbances. The proposed schemes achieve an intrinsic efficiency of $25\%$, which is compared with several existing protocols. The framework therefore provides a scalable and resource-efficient approach to unified quantum communication in realistic noisy quantum networks.

papers.title: Environment-assisted squeezing in a coherently driven non-Hermitian degenerate parametric oscillator
papers.abstract: Environment-assisted approaches to nonclassical light offer a practical path to strong squeezing in imperfect, lossy platforms. In this paper, we study a degenerate parametric oscillator in which a coherently driven cavity is coupled to a broadband squeezed reservoir via a single-port mirror. At the same time, the intracavity dynamics include non-Hermitian (gain-loss-imbalanced) terms. Within input--output theory, we obtain closed-form expressions for the steady-state quadrature variances, the output squeezing spectrum, and the power spectrum, and map their dependence on the reservoir squeeze factor, the coherent drive amplitude, and the parametric gain. We find that the non-Hermitian contributions open operating windows in which the intracavity quadrature noise is markedly suppressed below the standard quantum limit and, depending on the parameter set, either sharpen or amplify spectral squeezing and power-spectral features at the output. The non-Hermitian coefficients are treated as effective, low-order drift parameters that describe calibrated imbalance between engineered source and sink channels after auxiliary degrees of freedom have been eliminated. The analysis is restricted to the stable Gaussian regime in which the drift matrix is stable, and the squeezed-reservoir diffusion matrix remains physical. The results demonstrate an environment-assisted approach in which reservoir engineering and coherent driving work together to enhance squeezing. The resulting parameter maps identify experimentally testable windows, rather than a unique device prescription, for combining reservoir squeezing, coherent driving, and controlled gain/loss imbalance in cavity-QED and nonlinear photonic settings.

papers.title: Quantum Separability in Polynomial Time
papers.abstract: The quantum separability problem asks whether a bipartite density matrix is separable or is $η$-far from every separable state. We give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for this problem for every fixed constant gap $η>0$, when distance is measured in the Euclidean norm.

papers.title: Freezing Swampland: A Krylov Complexity Criterion for the Weak Gravity Conjecture
papers.abstract: We propose a quantum-information-theoretic perspective on the Weak Gravity Conjecture through the behavior of Krylov spread complexity. For a charged thermofield double state holographically dual to an AdS Reissner--Nordström black hole, we show that the extremal limit on the black-hole side is accompanied by an effective freezing of Krylov spreading. In this regime, the return amplitude becomes effectively a pure phase, and the dual quantum state ceases to spread nontrivially in Krylov space. We then incorporate charged matter and study the effect of Schwinger pair production in the near-horizon region. Within this semiclassical near-extremal analysis, the frozen behavior is lifted once the discharge channel is opened, and the dynamics become nontrivial again. This suggests that the Weak Gravity Conjecture may admit a complexity-based interpretation in terms of the absence of exact freezing in the presence of an available discharge channel. More broadly, our results point to a new connection between the swampland program, black-hole physics, and quantum information theory.

papers.title: The Physics of Unresolved Uncertainty: Quantum Mechanics as a Theory of Potentiality
papers.abstract: We propose a reformulation of quantum mechanics as a theory of unresolved uncertainty. This theory of potentiality is formulated in the language of complex-valued measure theory, regarded as a pre-probabilistic counterpart of ordinary probability theory. In this formulation, additivity, conditioning, independence, mixtures, transition kernels, and temporal divisibility retain natural linear forms at the potentiality level, while non-classical probability-level features such as interference arise from the nonlinear Born map. Measurement is described as Bayesian-type conditioning of potentialities on actualized information, and non-selective measurement as the replacement of coherent potentiality by statistical mixtures of conditional potentiality branches. Mixed states, decoherence, composite systems, entanglement, and Bell-type correlations are also given a unified potentiality-level interpretation. The density matrix is interpreted as a coherence kernel whose off-diagonal blocks encode retained phase relations. For pure bipartite states, potentiality independence is shown to be equivalent to factorization of the Born distribution in every pair of local contexts. The resulting formulation is empirically equivalent to standard quantum mechanics, but it makes explicit a pre-probabilistic description of physical reality that is usually implicit in the Hilbert-space formalism.

papers.title: Can PCE solve the factorisation problem via optimisation?
papers.abstract: The ongoing progress in quantum technologies has fueled a sustained exploration of their potential applications across various domains, particularly in computational problems that are considered intractable for classical systems. Among these problems, integer factorisation remains of special interest due to its relevance to widely used cryptographic schemes such as RSA. Among the different possibilities, one approach to factorisation is to convert the problem into a binary optimisation problem. However, current proposals usually need a large number of qubits that make them unfeasible within the current hardware. In this work, we investigate a possible adaptation of the Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) algorithm to the factorisation problem. Due to its compression capability, it can drastically reduce the number of needed qubits. The proposed approach explores how the structure and dynamics of the PCE framework may be employed to encode and analyze candidate factor relations within a quantum computational setting. Rather than presenting a replacement for established quantum factorisation methods, this study aims to provide a preliminary examination of the feasibility and limitations of the proposed adaptation. We discuss the algorithmic design, its conceptual relationship with existing quantum approaches, and the practical constraints associated with implementation on current or near-term quantum hardware. Initial observations suggest that the method may offer an alternative perspective for studying factorisation within the broader context of quantum computation, although no claim is made regarding computational advantage. These results are intended primarily as an exploratory contribution to ongoing research in quantum algorithms and computational number theory.

papers.title: Fixed points in de Finetti hierarchies
papers.abstract: De Finetti theorems convert permutation symmetry into approximate mixtures of product states and thereby justify a wide range of reductions in classical and quantum statistics. In this work we study de Finetti hierarchies in which the feasible states are additionally constrained to be fixed points of quantum channels, a condition that subsumes invariance under arbitrary compact symmetry groups. Combining the mean-ergodic theorem with the structure theory of conditional expectations, we prove a tight bound on the entanglement-assisted classical capacity of the dual of a conditional expectation, block-wise distortion bounds for informationally complete measurements adapted to fixed point algebras, and an exact type-based refinement of the chain rule for permutation-invariant states. From these tools we derive several de Finetti theorems: a double-sided extension theorem with $O\left(\sqrt{\log n}/n\right)$ convergence, an interpolation theorem whose dimension dependence is governed solely by the block structure of the fixed point algebras and which recovers the dimension-independent classical behavior for maximal tori, and a Bose-symmetric variant. Exploiting Schur-Weyl duality and Gelfand-Tsetlin bases, we further show that the rounding scheme producing certifiably good separable inner approximations for (constrained) separability problems can be implemented in time polynomial in $1/ε$ for fixed local dimensions, complementing the known efficient outer hierarchies. Applications to bilinear optimization under symmetries and to approximate quantum error correction are discussed.

papers.title: Qutrit-Based Neural Quantum Kernels for Classification Tasks
papers.abstract: Neural quantum kernels (NQKs) construct quantum kernels by pretraining a quantum neural network (QNN) and subsequently reusing the trained circuit as a task-adapted embedding. Extending this framework to qudits, with local unitaries in $\mathrm{SU}(d)$, provides a natural route to richer data embeddings through the increased local degrees of freedom and a direct interface for multiclass classification via intrinsically multi-level quantum systems. In this work, focusing on qutrits ($d=3$), we extend NQKs to the qudit setting and perform a systematic study of key design choices, including the number of encoded features, the number of qutrits, the kernel construction (1-to-$n$ and $n$-to-$n$), and the parameterization of $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ unitaries. Across binary and three-class tasks on four benchmark datasets, qutrit NQKs improve over the corresponding QNN baselines in nearly all settings considered and can benefit from scaling both the feature budget and the system size, although the magnitude of these gains may saturate, is dataset-dependent, and depends on the chosen parameterization. In particular, an ablation over $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ parameterizations shows that the unitary representation can substantially impact both optimization behaviour and classifier performance. These findings highlight the potential of qudit-based quantum models not only as a straightforward generalization of qubit-based architectures, but also as a promising means to better exploit complex data structures in quantum machine learning.

papers.title: Mitigation of Measurement-Induced State Transitions via a Fast-Load and Fast-Clear Readout
papers.abstract: High-fidelity and rapid qubit readout is essential for superconducting quantum processors, typically realized through the quantum non-demolition (QND) dispersive interaction within a qubit-resonator architecture. However, the achievable readout speed and fidelity are fundamentally limited by measurement-induced state transitions (MIST). For a transmon qubit, MIST is highly sensitive to the offset charge $n_g$ due to the charge dispersion of its higher-lying energy levels. In this work, we systematically investigate $n_g$-dependent MIST dynamics governed by the diabaticity and symmetry of pulse shaping within a charge-sensitive transmon architecture. We engineer fast-load and fast-clear pulses that effectively suppress resonator photon overshoots, thereby demonstrating a highly practical strategy to mitigate MIST without requiring complex waveforms or real-time feedback. Utilizing active gate-voltage control and rapid feedback, the measurement-induced transition probability is precisely mapped against $n_g$ and the steady-state resonator photon number, exhibiting strong agreement with numerical Floquet branch analysis. Ultimately, we evaluate the $n_g$-averaged total error probabilities for both readout and post-readout stages, verifying that a straightforward three-step pulse scheme consistently minimizes overall readout errors. Within the framework of large-scale superconducting quantum processors, this practical, hardware-free approach inherently offers a better trade-off between the readout signal-to-noise ratio and QND preservation.

papers.title: Neural Network Learning of One-Bit Protocols for Qubit Measurement Simulation
papers.abstract: Communication complexity provides a natural framework for quantifying the classical resources required to reproduce quantum statistics. In the qubit prepare-and-measure scenario, two classical bits have been shown to be necessary and sufficient to simulate arbitrary qubit states and arbi- trary quantum measurements exactly. However, this result does not exclude the possibility that restricted families of measurements may admit accurate 1-bit classical approximations. We use a neural network procedure to demonstrate that a single bit can achieve high average accuracy for specific measurement families. A performance analysis of our neural network reveals that symmet- ric measurements with uniformly weighted elements, such as those forming regular polyhedra, are particularly amenable to this restricted communication. By analyzing the patterns learned by the neural network, we derive an analytical protocol that is extremely accurate for finite information- ally complete symmetric configurations and becomes exact in the limit of a continuous isotropic measurement.

papers.title: Fast Trainable Multilinear Bases for Image Compression
papers.abstract: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), and their block-wise variants underpin most deployed image and video codecs. Their effectiveness rests on three properties: their runtime is near-linear (up to a polylogarithmic factor) in the image size, they are exactly invertible, and they carry few to no parameters. We generalize these transforms to dataset-adaptive isometric multilinear bases that keep all three properties at the cost of a polylogarithmic number of parameters, by parameterizing each basis as an isometric tensor network, inspired by quantum many-body theory, and training one shared basis per image dataset with Riemannian optimization. Because the family contains the DFT and the DCT-IV (a variant of the DCT) as exact points, training can start from these transforms, and it improves on its starting point at the compression level it is trained for. We evaluate the bases on natural photographs and line drawings. On photographs, which the cosine basis already fits well, the best trained basis leads the DCT only under aggressive truncation. On Quick Draw line drawings, under a common codec at matched quality, the best trained basis stores each image in about 20% fewer bytes than the 8x8 block cosine transform of the Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG) format, not counting the one-off storage of the basis.

papers.title: Optimal Dynamic Cooling of Multiple Qubits
papers.abstract: We solve the closed-system problem of cooling $M$ qubits, selected from $N$ identical thermal qubits, to the lowest common local temperature allowed by unitarity. The optimal protocol consists of two conceptually distinct steps. First, a passive rearrangement assigns the largest eigenvalues of the initial state to target sectors of lowest Hamming weight, thereby minimizing the total target energy. Second, a target-only complex-Hadamard transformation within each fixed-Hamming-weight subspace equalizes the one-qubit target marginals without changing any target-sector probability or the total energy. Consequently, imposing a common local temperature costs neither cooling depth nor additional work: the constrained optimum coincides with the unconstrained passive minimum for every $N>M$ and every initial temperature. The complex-Hadamard correction may nevertheless be costly at the circuit level. We therefore derive an exact arithmetic criterion for when the same optimum can be attained by a temperature-independent computational-basis permutation alone, and exhaustively classify the resulting finite-size islands of feasibility for $M+2\leq N\leq 128$. At isolated temperatures, further optimal permutations can arise through numerical cancellations between different thermal eigenvalue shells. These alternative realizations may reduce implementation complexity, but they cannot improve the cooling curve already attained by the universal protocol. We also derive the exact cooling curve, prove that at least two ancillary qubits are necessary and sufficient for nontrivial cooling, and show that joint many-target cooling can strictly outperform parallel single-target strategies.

papers.title: Effect of classical noises on the coherent population trapping based on the Green's function approach to the multiplicative stochastic processes
papers.abstract: Inspired by the Green's function (GF) approach in quantum field theory (QFT) and many body physics, we have developed a mathematical formalism to investigate classical multiplicative stochastic processes. Based on this approach, the interacting GF of any dynamical system subjected to classical stochastic noises, which enter into the system equations of motion in a multiplicative way, can be obtained from the noninteracting (free of noise) GF through an infinite perturbative series which may converge to an exact closed form under special conditions. Using this formalism, we have studied the effects of classical noises of the driving laser on the coherent population trapping (CPT) which have a crucial role in the performance of CPT-based atomic clocks. We have shown that if the bandwidth of the colored noise is sufficiently larger than the system damping rate, the infinite series corresponding to the interacting GF can be approximated by the closed form. The presented formalism enables us to investigate all kinds of homogeneous and inhomogeneous broadening mechanisms on the CPT transmission resonance lineshape, including dephasing due to atomic collisions, power/Doppler broadenings, as well as the broadening mechanisms due to phase and amplitude fluctuations of driving laser and compared their destructive effect with each other. It should be emphasized that the presented formalism is applicable to any dynamical system with multiplicative stochastic noises and the CPT phenomenon is just a prototype for the application of the presented formalism in practice.

papers.title: Performance and Stability of Quantum Krylov Diagonalization for the Hubbard Model
papers.abstract: Quantum Krylov diagonalization (QKD) has emerged as a promising hybrid quantum-classical approach for estimating ground-state properties of many-body systems on near-term quantum devices. In this work, we investigate the convergence, stability, and hardware performance of QKD for the one-dimensional Hubbard model with periodic boundary conditions. Building upon our previously developed low-depth Jordan--Wigner implementation, which reduces the number of two-qubit (CNOT) gates required for quantum time evolution, we perform a systematic study of the influence of the Krylov dimension, Hamiltonian evolution parameters, system size, interaction strength, and singular-value truncation (SVT) on the convergence of the method. Our results show that the performance of QKD is governed by a delicate interplay between the low-energy spectral structure of the Hamiltonian and numerical stability. In particular, systems with near-closing energy gaps require longer evolution times to efficiently resolve nearby eigenstates, while the evolution time, Krylov dimension, Trotter number, and SVT threshold must be carefully balanced to avoid numerical instabilities and accumulated time-discretization errors. This analysis provides practical guidelines for selecting algorithmic parameters in QKD. Finally, we demonstrate the algorithm on IBM quantum hardware, where the experimental results reproduce the convergence trends predicted by ideal simulations using only lightweight readout-error mitigation and a modest measurement budget. Together, these results demonstrate that QKD is a practical and hardware-efficient approach for studying strongly correlated fermionic systems on current NISQ quantum processors.

papers.title: An Integrated DFT-Wannier-Quantum Embedding Pipeline for Strongly Correlated Materials: Scaling Benchmarks in Li-hBN
papers.abstract: The seamless integration of Density Functional Theory (DFT) with quantum variational algorithms is essential for the predictive simulation of strongly correlated materials. In this work, we present an end-to-end computational pipeline - comprising DFT geometry relaxation, non-self-consistent field (NSCF) calculations, and Wannier-based orbital localization - to prepare active-space Hamiltonians for quantum embedding. We utilize the Adaptive Variational Quantum Eigensolver (ADAPT-VQE) framework, significantly enhanced by a Greedy-Operator Commutativity Partitioning (GOCP) approach and a Taylor-expanded O(5) operator evolution strategy to efficiently manage the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space. We demonstrate this framework through a systematic benchmark study of Li-hBN, mapping the system onto qubit registers and investigating the convergence behavior as the active space is expanded from 8 to 14 spatial orbitals. Our results quantify the relationship between active-space size and computational demand, identifying a critical "scaling wall" where classical simulation costs transition from manageable to intractable. This study provides a rigorous performance baseline for the DFT-to-ADAPT-VQE workflow and offers empirical insights into the memory and processing limits currently facing hybrid quantum-classical architectures using advanced co-processing strategies.

papers.title: Permutationally Invariant Quantum State Tomography for Fermions
papers.abstract: Quantum state tomography provides complete information about a quantum state, but its measurement cost generally grows exponentially with system size. In many-particle quantum simulators, this challenge is further compounded by the limited accessibility of local measurements and controls. Here we develop a tomography protocol for permutation-invariant fermionic many-body states with U(1) particle-number symmetry. We show that any such state is completely determined by the distribution of the total particle number and the occupation of a single collective mode within each particle-number sector, both of which are accessible in current ultracold-atom experiments. The number of required observables scales only linearly with the system size. More generally, the protocol reconstructs the permutation-symmetrized component of arbitrary U(1)-symmetric fermionic states, which can still encode nontrivial many-body and state-level structure beyond conventional few-body observables. We demonstrate this protocol in interacting non-Gaussian states of the complex Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and in free-fermion chains across a Lifshitz transition. This framework opens a route toward information-theoretic characterization of strongly correlated itinerant quantum matter in experimentally realistic fermionic quantum simulators.

papers.title: Generalized Mermin Inequalities for Benchmarking Large-Scale GHZ States
papers.abstract: Multipartite Bell tests provide a correlation-only route to benchmarking quantum processors, but their application at large scales is hindered by the rapid decay of many-body correlators under noise and exponentially many terms in conventional Bell expressions. Here we address these scalability obstacles by introducing a finite-setting generalized Mermin family of state-tailored Bell inequalities with analytic certification bounds, in which the measurement-setting number $m$ provides an additional certification dimension complementary to the system size $n$. We show that, for the powers-of-two setting choices considered here, increasing $m$ leaves the ideal normalized multipartite quantum value unchanged while lowering the relevant classical bounds, thereby strengthening the Bell-violation ratios and yielding an improved noise-robustness scaling compared to the standard Mermin inequality. We test this construction experimentally on a programmable superconducting processor by preparing Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states of up to 80 qubits. Using randomized sampling for direct Bell-operator estimation, we observe Bell ratios that grow exponentially with system size, certify a nonlocality depth of 14, and show that increasing $m$ strengthens both the Bell ratio and depth certification. All results are obtained solely from measured correlators and analytical bounds, without readout correction, tomography, or model-based mitigation. Generalized Mermin inequalities therefore provide a sharper Bell benchmark for noisy large-scale GHZ states.

papers.title: Quantum Speed Limits and the Ultimate Scaling of the Quantum Sensors
papers.abstract: Quantum metrology promises sensitivity beyond classical strategies, yet it remains unsettled how quantum-enabled precision should scale with physical resources and how to interpret quantum advantage. We provide a physically grounded resource accounting that clarifies the true Heisenberg limit and resolves apparent super-Heisenberg paradoxes. We demonstrate that the Heisenberg limit is best viewed as an information-theoretic manifestation of the quantum speed limit. We illustrate these ideas with a simple, super-resolving phase-estimation protocol based on Rabi oscillations in two-level atoms driven on an $m$-photon resonance. In this setting, the phase error scales as $n^{-m/2}$, where $n$ is the average photon number. Recasting metrological sensitivity through quantum dynamical speed limits yields operational bounds that reconcile such super-resolution strategies with the standard Heisenberg interpretation and identify the relevant resources in the norm of the generator. We also revisit the common attribution of the NOON state's $1/n$ scaling to quantum entanglement. We show that such an attribution is not generic and the Heisenberg $1/n$ scaling does not, by itself, certify entanglement as the enabling resource.

papers.title: A Probabilistic Representation for Multi-State Discrete-time Quantum Walks
papers.abstract: Building upon the pioneering framework of Vu (2026), we construct a probabilistic representation for three-state discrete-time quantum walks on integer lattices and validate it through empirical examples. Furthermore, we establish that this representation converges to the continuum solution of multi-state Dirac partial differential equations. Broadly, our findings demonstrate that this probabilistic paradigm serves as a robust alternative for simulating higher-dimensional quantum walks, opening new theoretical avenues to analyze quantum dynamics using classical stochastic processes.

papers.title: A TQFT-based Platform for Efficient Computation of Knot Invariants
papers.abstract: We present an interactive web platform that unifies the construction Feynman ribbon diagrams (FRDs), the evaluation of higher-rank Chern--Simons knot invariants, and the identification of FRD-like knots at higher crossing numbers. These tree-structured diagrams naturally represent arborescent knots, which we refer to throughout as FRD-like knots. Within a single visual environment, users can construct an FRD as a tensor network, evaluate its associated Chern--Simons invariants, and use the resulting invariant data to distinguish and identify the corresponding knot. To our knowledge, this is the first platform to combine diagrammatic construction, tensor-network evaluation, invariant computation, and knot identification within a unified workflow.

papers.title: Observation of an emergent energy scale close to dimensional reduction in a quasi-two-dimensional quantum magnet
papers.abstract: By appropriately perturbing a critical transverse-field Ising chain away from its critical point, the system can develop a finite correlation length with a characteristic purely massive spectrum, whose ratios and correlations are precisely described by an integrable field theory and an infinite set of integrals of motion corresponding to the $E_8$ Lie algebra. In this work, we report on experimental observation of a characteristic massive spectrum close to transverse field-induced dimensional reduction in a quasi-two-dimensional quantum magnet Cu$_2$(OH)$_3$Br, providing evidence for an emergent $E_8$ symmetry and the corresponding excitations of bound states in the sublattice of its ferromagnetic chains. These results demonstrate the power of integrable field theory in describing emergent many-body quantum critical phenomena in condensed matter systems.

papers.title: Dynamical control of particle jets from a driven condensate in a one-dimensional lattice with double-well potential
papers.abstract: We investigate the nonlinear dynamics of a Bose-Einstein condensate trapped in a double-well potential of a one-dimensional lattice, where the interatomic interactions are periodically modulated in time. In the typical case of a symmetric double-well, we observe collective particle emission under resonant driving, where the excitation regimes are explicitly constrained by the interplay between the drive strength and the hopping amplitude. By introducing a depth asymmetry between the wells, we find that moderate bias specifically enhances the emission rate, while large asymmetry suppresses it. The particle jets can be further controlled by modulating the hopping amplitudes, where the emission is weakened for finite hopping imbalances. These results outline the roles of asymmetry and external driving in precisely manipulating quantum many-body transport, and may offer insights into the design of atomtronic devices.

papers.title: One Aperture, Two Colors: Depth-Allocated Bilayer Silicon Nitride Gratings for Trapped-Ion Addressing
papers.abstract: Scaling multicolor quantum control on chip presents a geometric conflict: each added wavelength traditionally requires another routing corridor, emitter, and electrode opening, consuming trap-surface area and exposing charge-susceptible dielectric near the quantum target. This work introduces an all-planar, vertically stacked silicon-nitride architecture that co-registers independently fed optical transitions within one 24 x 24 $μ$m footprint. For $^{40}\text{Ca}^+$, the device focuses the 729.4 nm qubit and 854.2 nm repump wavelengths onto a shared site 70 $μ$m above the upper film. A hierarchical design combines a differentiable cell search for a three-level scatterer, analytic confocal phase synthesis, and deterministic depth allocation across two etches per layer, preserving an explicit 125 nm propagation-axis line-and-space floor without grayscale patterning. Retargeting the upper-layer phase co-registers the focal maxima to within 0.1 $μ$m in mesh-converged Tidy3D and independently constructed Lumerical FDTD models, retaining >99.9% of each color's peak intensity at the common coordinate with focusing efficiencies of 0.410 and 0.168. At 5 $μ$m ion spacing, the qubit channel reaches -24.8 dB point crosstalk, remains below -18.0 dB across a 0.5 $μ$m-radius positioning disk, and yields -23.0 dB symmetric-traceless field-gradient suppression. In the analytic House conductor geometry, the shared footprint provides 15.3 $μ$m clearance to the nearest radio-frequency rail with zero RF-null displacement. By uniting separate optical inputs and transition-specific wavefronts within one ion-facing aperture, this hierarchy establishes a transferable template for addressing other atomic wavelength pairs and dense multicolor quantum interfaces.

papers.title: Topology-dependent relativistic degradation of multipartite entanglement
papers.abstract: The influence of relativistic motion on quantum entanglement is commonly attributed to acceleration-induced thermal noise. Here we show that, for asymmetric multipartite states, the topology of entanglement can become equally important. Considering a three-qubit Star state in the Unruh-DeWitt detector framework, we compare two inequivalent acceleration configurations in which either the central or a peripheral qubit undergoes uniform acceleration. We demonstrate that these physically equivalent accelerations lead to qualitatively different entanglement dynamics: acceleration of a peripheral qubit induces a revival of one-tangle that is absent when the central qubit accelerates, whereas genuine tripartite entanglement decays monotonically but with markedly different robustness. Our results uncover a topology-dependent mechanism for relativistic entanglement degradation, showing that the response of multipartite quantum correlations is determined jointly by Unruh thermalization and the structural role of the accelerated subsystem. This work identifies asymmetric quantum networks as a distinct platform for controlling relativistic quantum resources.

papers.title: Lossless Address Coding for Quantum Networks
papers.abstract: As quantum systems advance toward interconnected architectures, the ability to identify nodes, manage resources, and support network-level functions becomes increasingly critical. In this work, we propose a lossless source coding scheme for addressing in quantum networks that enables compact, hierarchical, and coherently processable quantum address states. Specifically, we introduce a prefix-suffix address space and develop an isometric hierarchical encoder-decoder that guarantees unique decodability. We further provide a practical Huffman-based procedure that embeds prefix-free, length-eigenstate codewords into the address space, thereby preserving isometry. The scheme is particularly designed for networks with hierarchical structure, heterogeneous cluster sizes, and configurable address assignment to accommodate dynamic network conditions. A numerical example on a 13-node network demonstrates that the proposed hierarchical encoding scheme is feasible and achieves perfect fidelity. This work establishes a rigorous connection between source coding theory and quantum network design, offering a practical framework towards scalable and coherent quantum addressing.

papers.title: Current cross-correlations as probes for poor man's Majorana states
papers.abstract: The minimal Kitaev chain that emulates a topological superconductor with three quantum dots offers a tunable platform for potentially hosting poor man's Majorana (PMM) modes. Asserting the need to go beyond differential conductance spectroscopy, we introduce current-current correlations as a viable framework for verifying their true non-locality. The robustness of the PMM modes, specifically with respect to delocalization as the system is tuned away from sweet spots, we show, is embedded in the relative magnitudes of the nonlocal transport processes. This aspect is adeptly captured by current cross-correlations, whose features show remarkable stability around the PMM sweet spot, specifically with respect to the detuning of an outer dot. We establish this as a prominent feature and a diagnostic for true PMMs even in the short chain limit. Our results accentuate the need for current cross-correlation measurements as a diagnostic framework for unambiguously verifying true non-locality of entangled states as well as topologically protected states.

papers.title: Photon pair antibunching and second-order correlations between pair events
papers.abstract: We introduce the pair second-order correlation function $g_{\textrm{pairs}}^{\left(2\right)}=\left\langle \left(P^{\dagger}\right)^{2}P^{2}\right\rangle /\left\langle P^{\dagger}P\right\rangle ^{2}$, defined through the pair operator $P^{\dagger}=a^{\dagger}b^{\dagger}$, to characterize second-order correlations and pair bunching and antibunching in photon-pair creation processes. This quantity directly probes correlations between pair-generation events within a single two-mode quantum state, providing access to the intrinsic pair-generation process beyond conventional single-mode or heralded second-order correlations, which do not directly capture correlations between pair events.
